question: Do the toy-function and neural-network experiments establish that Stochastic Average Gradient, plus the proposed SAG-momentum and SAG-Adam combinations, converge faster or perform better than standard optimizers?

key_findings.claim: The paper's proved result is the original convex SAG guarantee, not a convergence result for either proposed hybrid or for the non-convex experiments.
key_findings.evidence: Section 5 states the smooth convex and strongly convex SAG theorem and explicitly sends the proof to Schmidt et al. (2013), while Section 8 says the momentum and Adam combinations are only empirical illustrations and leaves their expected convergence rates to future work. The theorem therefore does not justify claims about the log Rosenbrock, log Rastrigin, multilayer perceptron, or convolutional settings.

anchors.section: Section 5, proof attribution and rate discussion

key_findings.claim: No presented experiment cleanly tests the defining stale per-component gradient memory of SAG.
key_findings.evidence: The two toy objectives are each passed to the released optimizer as n=m=1, so the stored-gradient update telescopes to the current gradient and is ordinary gradient descent; the named SAG-momentum and SAG-Adam variants similarly reduce to current-gradient momentum/adaptive updates. The released experiment shell uses a training batch size of 512. Against the paper's 80% training sizes, wine, iris, Boston, diabetes, and Linnerud each fit in one batch and again collapse to full-gradient behavior. Digits is the sole plotted dataset with multiple batches, but it enters the incorrect mini-batch accumulator described separately.

key_findings.claim: The linked implementation's default stored-sum estimator is mathematically wrong whenever more than one mini-batch is used.
key_findings.evidence: The paper links Tikquuss/sag_torch as its reproducibility artifact. At audited commit a4f5b1baa48ff449b15c604956e54da306d96ef5, the default with_d=True path subtracts the old batch contribution divided by the number of seen samples or batches but adds the new aggregate batch gradient without the matching weight. In non-batch mode it also copies one aggregate batch gradient into every sample slot rather than computing per-example gradients. A two-equal-batch scalar probe with successive aggregate gradients 2 and 4 produces stored direction 6, whereas their correct average is 3. Thus the digits curves do not evaluate the SAG estimator written in the paper.

anchors.section: Mini-batches for vectorized computation and reduced storage

key_findings.claim: The toy-function plots cannot support optimizer rankings because they do not isolate SAG, do not tune baselines, and derive headline summaries from manually entered values.
key_findings.evidence: The tracked toy notebook gives every optimizer the same learning rate 0.001, sets weight decay to 1.0 for nearly all methods despite their different coupled or decoupled semantics, and gives Rprop no comparable decay. Its current training loop is 10,000 steps, yet the prose compares some methods at 100,000 or 400,000 iterations. The final-error and convergence-speed bars are built from hand-entered dictionaries rather than computed from saved runs; the notebook has no stored execution outputs. The paper itself calls convergence speed an approximation of the iteration where stabilization occurs and gives no algorithmic threshold.

anchors.section: Rosenbrock qualitative rankings and stabilization definition

key_findings.claim: Several mathematical descriptions of the toy landscapes are incorrect and obscure what the experiments actually test.
key_findings.evidence: A monotone logarithm preserves the location and number of local extrema, so it does not create the ravine or local minima attributed to it. The two-dimensional Rosenbrock function used here has one global minimum rather than a global minimum surrounded along its ravine by many local minima. Rastrigin is multimodal, not 'unimodal (in terms of global minimum).' Earlier, the paper also equates a singular Hessian with an undefined Hessian, and later lists feed-forward neural networks as linearly parameterized models whose SAG memory can be reduced to one scalar per example; neither statement is generally true.

anchors.section: Structured gradients and claimed linearly parameterized examples

key_findings.claim: The scikit-learn protocol offers neither an independent test set nor uncertainty, and its preprocessing leaks validation information.
key_findings.evidence: The paper uses a single 80/20 train-validation split and reports 2,000-epoch curves for six tiny datasets, without a test partition, number of seeds, confidence intervals, or significance analysis. The linked code standardizes all samples before the random split, fitting mean and variance with validation data. It saves checkpoints selected by the same validation metric later plotted as performance, so the displayed validation value is also the model-selection target. Every optimizer receives the same nominal learning rate rather than a documented tuning budget.

key_findings.claim: The visual result record contains exact duplicates and missing headline charts, making even the plotted evidence internally unreliable.
key_findings.evidence: All 52 figures were rendered and compared. After excluding captions, the wine and iris convergence-speed plots in Figures 16 and 23 are pixel-identical, as are their steady-state plots in Figures 17 and 24. Page 28 prints captions for digits Figures 30 and 31 but contains no corresponding bar charts. Several regression steady-state panels use a 0-100 display visually resembling classification accuracy, yet no numerical result table defines the plotted values. The dense legends and axes are frequently too small to audit from the paper.

key_findings.claim: The TorchVision section reports a setup but no results, and the released CIFAR-100 path silently loads CIFAR-10 data.
key_findings.evidence: Section 7.2.2 lists MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 plus a small CNN, but the paper ends immediately afterward without a curve, table, metric, or conclusion for any of them. Table 3 also gives Fashion-MNIST a total size of 7,000 while its listed train and validation sizes sum to 70,000. In the linked code, the cifar100 branch instantiates torchvision.datasets.CIFAR10 for both train and validation while declaring 100 output classes, so a nominal CIFAR-100 run is invalid.

key_findings.claim: The release is inspectable but not a safe or self-contained reproduction package.
key_findings.evidence: All ordinary Python files compile syntactically, but the repository has no tests, continuous integration, license, environment lock, checkpoints, result logs, or committed numeric tables. requirements.txt omits central imports including PyTorch, torchvision, NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, Plotly, and labellines. The initialization option computes its running mean incorrectly, SAGSGDWithd applies decoupled weight decay twice, the deterministic cuDNN flag is misspelled, and current scikit-learn no longer provides load_boston. Two tracked notebooks expose the same plaintext W&B credential, which should be revoked and purged rather than reused.

key_findings.claim: The proposed momentum and Adam combinations are not positioned against the primary variance-reduction literature, including a nearly simultaneous direct competitor.
key_findings.evidence: The related-work section surveys standard optimizers but omits SAGA, SVRG, Katyusha, SARAH, SPIDER, SpiderBoost, and adaptive variance-reduction methods. Katyusha and SpiderBoost already combine momentum with variance reduction and provide convergence analyses. AdaLVR was submitted three days before this paper and combines AdaGrad with SAGA or loopless SVRG, supplies convex theory, and explicitly reports empirical RMSprop- and Adam-plus-variance-reduction variants. The present hybrids have neither such theory nor a functioning experiment that isolates variance reduction.

key_findings.claim: The paper correctly identifies SAG's per-example memory as a major obstacle, but supplies no evidence that its hybrids are viable at modern scale.
key_findings.evidence: The conclusion calls SAG's memory cost very high and impractical for large-scale use. The paper gives no wall-clock time, peak memory, gradient-oracle count, model-size sweep, or distributed experiment. Its only purported image experiments have no reported outcome, while current recursive estimators such as SARAH, SPIDER, and MARS avoid an n-by-parameter gradient table. A claim of better machine-learning optimization therefore remains restricted to the paper's small, compromised demonstrations.

method.core_idea: Empirically compare the original Stochastic Average Gradient optimizer with common PyTorch optimizers, then replace each stored SAG component by a momentum-transformed or Adam-preconditioned component to form sag_sgd and sag_adam.
method.mechanism: Vanilla SAG maintains a stale gradient y_i for every finite-sum component and updates parameters with their average after refreshing one component or mini-batch. The proposed momentum hybrid stores a velocity-like transformation for the selected component before averaging; the Adam hybrid stores a first-moment term divided element-wise by the square root of its second-moment term. The paper imports the original SAG convex theorem, describes implementation heuristics, plots two two-dimensional log-transformed objectives, trains a small MLP on six scikit-learn datasets, and specifies a CNN for four TorchVision datasets.
assumptions: The released optimizer implements the same per-component average as the SAG equations.
A batch aggregate gradient can stand in for every sample's component gradient without changing the estimator.
The n=1 toy objectives reveal benefits from SAG's stale-gradient memory.
Full-batch training on tiny datasets reveals benefits from stochastic variance reduction.
One shared learning rate and mostly shared weight decay constitute a fair optimizer comparison.
Different optimizers' coupled and decoupled weight-decay implementations optimize comparable objectives.
A manually approximated stabilization iteration is a reproducible convergence-speed metric.
One train-validation split and an unspecified number of runs characterize general performance.
Using the same validation set for model selection and reporting does not bias the reported value.
Scaling all data before splitting does not leak validation statistics.
A monotone log transformation changes the count or nature of local optima in the claimed way.
The original smooth convex SAG theorem is informative for non-convex neural networks and the proposed hybrids without a new analysis.
The O(n times parameter-count) gradient table is affordable for the intended models.
Plots without numerical tables or saved run artifacts are sufficient to verify rankings.
A listed but unreported TorchVision setup contributes evidence for large-scale use.

techniques.role: Stores a stale gradient for each finite-sum component and steps along their running average.
Normalizes by the number of components seen so far instead of the full n during initialization.
Refreshes a group of component memories per vectorized mini-batch.
Stores momentum-transformed selected gradients before forming the SAG direction.
Stores Adam-style moment-preconditioned selected gradients before forming the SAG direction.
Visualizes optimizer trajectories on logarithms of two-dimensional Rosenbrock and Rastrigin objectives.
Plots grouped validation trajectories and hand summarized speed and steady-state bars across optimizers.

evaluations.setting: Two-dimensional logarithmic Rosenbrock objective initialized at (-3, 6), with n=m=1 in the linked SAG implementation.
evaluations.metric: Trajectory, Euclidean distance to the global minimizer, and manually approximated iteration of stabilization.
evaluations.result: The paper says SAG reaches the ravine in fewer than 1,000 iterations versus more than 100,000 for Adadelta and Adagrad, while several adaptive methods eventually reach the minimum and SAG does not; sag_sgd is reported faster than SAG and sag_adam nearly reaches the minimum.
evaluations.baseline: SGD, momentum, Nesterov, ASGD, RMSprop variants, Rprop, Adadelta, Adagrad, Adam variants, and the two hybrids; the n=1 SAG path is ordinary current-gradient descent and the release hard-codes the aggregate bars.

evaluations.setting: Two-dimensional logarithmic Rastrigin objective initialized at (-4, 2), again with n=m=1.
evaluations.metric: Trajectory, Euclidean distance to the global minimizer, and manually approximated stabilization iteration.
evaluations.result: The paper says SAG moves from its first local basin in fewer than 1,000 iterations versus up to 400,000 for Adagrad, and reports sag_adam as one of the closest methods to the global optimum; it also says no optimizer reaches that optimum.
evaluations.baseline: The same optimizer family, with one nominal learning rate, inconsistent effective regularization, no persisted run output, and no actual SAG variance-reduction mechanism at n=1.

evaluations.setting: A width-50 Leaky-ReLU MLP with dropout 0.1 trained for 2,000 epochs on 80/20 splits of wine, iris, digits, Boston housing, diabetes, and Linnerud.
evaluations.metric: Plotted training and validation loss plus classification accuracy or regression error, with aggregate convergence-speed and steady-state bar charts.
evaluations.result: The conclusion says SAG outperforms a majority of compared algorithms and that the momentum and Adam combinations improve speed and performance. No numerical result table, uncertainty, independent test set, or aggregate cross-dataset statistic is supplied; wine and iris aggregate bars are exact duplicates and the two digits aggregate bars are absent.
evaluations.baseline: Sixteen standard or custom optimizer labels plus SAG and its hybrids. Five datasets are full-batch under the released 512 batch size, and digits is processed by the invalid multi-batch estimator.

evaluations.setting: A two-convolution, two-linear-layer classifier specified for MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100.
evaluations.result: The paper provides dataset sizes and architecture only, then moves directly to the conclusion. No TorchVision experiment, curve, table, checkpoint, or claimed number appears.
evaluations.baseline: No optimizer comparison is reported; the release's CIFAR-100 branch loads CIFAR-10 while declaring 100 classes.

evaluations.setting: Static and arithmetic audit of the linked sag_torch repository at current HEAD a4f5b1baa48ff449b15c604956e54da306d96ef5.
evaluations.metric: Syntax compilation, estimator invariants, minimal scalar update probes, dependency completeness, tests, artifacts, and secret scan.
evaluations.result: Python compilation passes, but a two-mini-batch probe returns an unnormalized sum rather than the required average; the initialization mean and double weight decay contain additional defects. The project lacks tests, CI, a complete environment, license, and result artifacts, and tracked notebooks contain a plaintext service credential.
evaluations.baseline: The paper's Algorithm 1 invariant that d equals the sum of stored component gradients and the update divides that sum by the appropriate component count.

limitations: Author-stated: SAG's memory cost is very high compared with other algorithms and makes it impractical at large scale.
Author-stated: convergence rates for sag_sgd and sag_adam are not analyzed and are left to future work.
Reviewer inference: the imported SAG theorem covers smooth convex finite sums, not the non-convex toy and neural-network objectives used for the claims.
Reviewer inference: n=1 and full-batch experiments eliminate the stale-component variance-reduction mechanism the study purports to compare.
Reviewer inference: the only reported multi-batch task uses a released estimator that fails the SAG averaging invariant.
Reviewer inference: no learning-rate or optimizer-specific hyperparameter tuning protocol is reported.
Reviewer inference: one 80/20 split, no independent test set, unspecified replicates, and no confidence intervals preclude general performance claims.
Reviewer inference: StandardScaler is fitted before the split and the validation metric is used both to select and report checkpoints.
Reviewer inference: aggregate toy metrics are manually entered and the tracked notebook stores no outputs from the underlying runs.
Reviewer inference: exact duplicate wine and iris figures, missing digits aggregate charts, and no numeric tables make the visual evidence unreliable.
Reviewer inference: no outcome is reported for any TorchVision dataset despite their inclusion in the methods section.
Reviewer inference: no time, memory, gradient-count, energy, or model-scale benchmark supports efficiency.
Reviewer inference: the linked environment omits required dependencies and supplies no tests, CI, lockfile, checkpoints, or logs.
Reviewer inference: a tracked plaintext W&B credential is a security defect and must be revoked and removed from history.
Reviewer inference: the paper omits foundational and contemporary variance-reduction competitors, including direct momentum and adaptive hybrids.
Reviewer inference: arXiv flags substantial text overlap with the original SAG paper, consistent with Sections 1-6 largely recapitulating prior exposition and theorem statements.
failure_modes: A one-component or one-batch objective makes SAG telescope to the current gradient, so a reported win is falsely attributed to variance reduction.
An unnormalized sum of batch-average gradients grows with the number of seen batches and changes the effective learning rate within an epoch.
Copying one mini-batch gradient into every per-sample slot destroys the component-gradient memory SAG theory assumes.
Unequal final batch sizes weight batches equally or inconsistently instead of weighting individual examples correctly.
The current-gradient toy optimizer looks like SAG in legends while behaving as gradient descent, momentum, or an Adam-like update.
A shared learning rate favors one optimizer family and makes slower competitors appear intrinsically worse.
Different weight-decay semantics or double-applied decay change the objective being optimized across methods.
A manually chosen stabilization point converts subjective visual judgment into an apparently quantitative speed claim.
Validation leakage and checkpoint selection inflate apparent generalization on tiny datasets.
One split or random order reverses rankings that lack repeated-run uncertainty.
A duplicated or missing plot propagates the wrong dataset's results under a new caption.
The n-by-parameter gradient table exhausts accelerator memory long before a modern model can be tested.
An incomplete requirements file prevents a clean reproduction even though individual source files compile.
The CIFAR-100 branch trains a 100-class head on CIFAR-10 labels and yields meaningless comparisons.
An exposed experiment-tracking token permits unauthorized access until revoked.
reusable_insights: Before benchmarking a variance-reduced optimizer, assert that the experiment has at least two independently refreshed finite-sum components and test the stored-estimator invariant every step.
Define whether a component is an example or a mini-batch; compute per-example gradients or derive a correctly weighted mini-batch estimator rather than silently mixing the two.
Include degeneration tests proving that one-component SAG equals gradient descent and that equal component gradients reproduce the full gradient.
Use tiny arithmetic unit tests with unequal batch sizes to catch normalization errors before expensive training.
Tune each optimizer under the same budget and report the search space, best configuration, and sensitivity rather than forcing one learning rate on all methods.
Separate regularization from optimizer mechanics and match coupled or decoupled decay semantics across baselines.
Compute convergence time from a preregistered threshold or area-under-curve statistic, not manual visual stabilization labels.
Fit preprocessing only on training data and reserve a final test set that is untouched by checkpoint selection.
Report per-seed raw trajectories, central tendency, uncertainty, and paired comparisons in numeric tables alongside figures.
Generate every summary plot from immutable result files with dataset IDs embedded in provenance, then test for accidental duplicate image payloads.
Benchmark gradient-oracle calls, wall-clock time, peak memory, and final held-out quality together; optimizer speed is a Pareto question.
Compare table-memory methods with low-memory recursive estimators such as SARAH, SPIDER, and MARS when scale is a target.
Pin a complete environment, add estimator-level tests and CI, and publish compact logs and checkpoints for at least one deterministic reproduction.
Scan notebooks and history for credentials before release; revoke any discovered token rather than merely deleting the visible cell.
open_questions: Do correctly implemented sag_sgd and sag_adam improve oracle complexity or wall-clock convergence on any non-convex problem under explicit assumptions?
What precise estimator do the proposed hybrids average: raw component gradients, momentum states, bias-corrected moments, or preconditioned directions?
Can either hybrid be made unbiased, or can its bias be bounded tightly enough for useful convergence theory?
How should first- and second-moment states be indexed when examples are reshuffled into changing mini-batches?
Can a low-memory recursive estimator retain the intended momentum or Adam behavior without an n-by-parameter table?
Do the hybrids beat tuned SAGA, loopless SVRG, Katyusha, SpiderBoost, AdaSpider, AdaLVR, and MARS at matched oracle and memory budgets?
Do any advantages survive on standard convex finite-sum benchmarks where SAG's assumptions actually hold?
Do any advantages survive on modern non-convex vision or language models across at least five seeds?
How sensitive are rankings to learning rate, batch size, momentum, beta values, initialization, and regularization semantics?
What happens when batch sizes are unequal, batches are reshuffled, or data sampling is non-uniform?
Can automated estimator-invariant tests detect every divergence between the equations and a vectorized implementation?
What performance-memory frontier is possible with compressed, factored, quantized, or sketched component memories?
Why are the wine and iris aggregate plots identical, and can the raw run records reconstruct the correct figures?
Were any TorchVision runs completed, and if so, where are their metrics and why are they absent from the paper?

competitive_landscape.title: Minimizing Finite Sums with the Stochastic Average Gradient
competitive_landscape.difference: Schmidt, Le Roux, and Bach introduce SAG, prove its sublinear and strongly convex linear rates, discuss mini-batches, regularization, storage, and initialization, and provide controlled finite-sum experiments. The present paper imports that theorem and much of the exposition, then attempts a PyTorch empirical comparison and two unproved hybrids.

competitive_landscape.title: SAGA: A Fast Incremental Gradient Method With Support for Non-Strongly Convex Composite Objectives
competitive_landscape.difference: SAGA corrects and simplifies the gradient-table estimator, supplies stronger convergence theory, and directly supports non-strongly-convex composite objectives. It is a necessary baseline for any claim that a new stored-gradient optimizer improves SAG, but it is absent from this paper.

competitive_landscape.title: Accelerating Stochastic Gradient Descent using Predictive Variance Reduction
competitive_landscape.difference: SVRG periodically uses a reference full gradient and stochastic correction instead of storing one full gradient per example. It is a canonical variance-reduction baseline with a different memory-computation tradeoff that the paper never tests despite acknowledging SAG's prohibitive table memory.

competitive_landscape.title: Katyusha: The First Direct Acceleration of Stochastic Gradient Methods
competitive_landscape.difference: Katyusha develops a dedicated negative-momentum mechanism on top of Nesterov momentum and variance reduction, with optimal accelerated convex finite-sum rates and mini-batch scaling. It predates sag_sgd and shows that merely combining the names SAG and momentum is not the relevant novelty bar.

competitive_landscape.title: SARAH: A Novel Method for Machine Learning Problems Using Stochastic Recursive Gradient
competitive_landscape.difference: SARAH recursively updates a variance-reduced estimator without storing all past component gradients and proves strongly convex linear convergence. It directly addresses the large-memory limitation admitted by the paper and should replace standard Adam variants as a primary comparison for scalable variance reduction.

competitive_landscape.title: SpiderBoost and Momentum: Faster Stochastic Variance Reduction Algorithms
competitive_landscape.difference: SpiderBoost supplies a constant-step recursive variance-reduction method for composite non-convex optimization and a momentum acceleration with near-optimal oracle complexity and experiments. It is a much closer comparator to sag_sgd than ordinary momentum SGD, yet receives no discussion.

competitive_landscape.title: Adaptive Stochastic Variance Reduction for Non-convex Finite-Sum Minimization
competitive_landscape.difference: AdaSpider combines an AdaGrad-inspired adaptive step size with a SPIDER estimator and proves near-optimal non-convex finite-sum complexity without prior smoothness or accuracy parameters. It directly demonstrates the theory and non-convex positioning missing from the proposed adaptive hybrid.

competitive_landscape.title: Finite-sum optimization: Adaptivity to smoothness and loopless variance reduction
competitive_landscape.difference: AdaLVR was submitted three days before this paper. It combines AdaGrad with SAGA or loopless SVRG, proves a smooth-convex gradient complexity without knowing the smoothness constant, and empirically combines RMSprop and Adam with variance-reduced estimators. This is the closest primary competitor to sag_adam and sets a substantially higher theory and implementation bar.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Ineffectiveness of Variance Reduced Optimization for Deep Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Defazio and Bottou test why classical variance-reduced methods often fail to improve modern deep-learning training. That negative evidence makes it essential to demonstrate true component variance reduction, tuned baselines, and scale; the present n=1, full-batch, and invalid multi-batch experiments do not meet that burden.

competitive_landscape.title: MARS: Unleashing the Power of Variance Reduction for Training Large Models
competitive_landscape.difference: MARS reconciles recursive variance reduction with AdamW, Lion, and Shampoo-style preconditioning through scaled stochastic recursive momentum, then evaluates GPT-2 models up to 770M parameters. It is current evidence that adaptive variance reduction can be framed without an n-by-parameter table and tested at a scale absent here.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims a broad empirical comparison in which SAG converges faster on two toy problems and performs better than many common machine-learning optimizers, and introduces SAG combined with momentum and with Adam to improve convergence speed and final performance.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The two hybrid update forms are written explicitly and the paper contains extensive trajectory and learning-curve panels. It also links a PyTorch repository, allowing the proposed implementations and plotting workflow to be inspected.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The only plausible new element is the particular choice to store momentum- or Adam-transformed directions in a SAG-like table. The paper supplies no convergence analysis for it, omits older direct momentum and adaptive variance-reduction work, and was preceded by AdaLVR's much closer Adam/RMSprop-plus-variance-reduction study. More importantly, the linked experiments never provide a valid test of the proposed mechanism: toy and five tabular settings collapse to current/full-gradient updates, while the only multi-batch setting uses a wrong accumulator. Hand-entered summaries, duplicated and missing figures, leakage, no independent test results, and no TorchVision outcomes further remove empirical support. arXiv's substantial-text-overlap notice with the original SAG paper reinforces that the recapitulated theorem and exposition are not novel. The work is best treated as an inspectable but failed pilot implementation, not evidence for a new competitive optimizer.

reviewer_notes: Read all 37 pages of the hashed arXiv v1 source submitted 2023-07-27, including every displayed update, theorem, implementation heuristic, experiment caption, all 52 figures, all three tables, the conclusion, and both reference pages. Rendered and visually inspected every page. Exact image-crop comparison found Figures 16 and 23 pixel-identical and Figures 17 and 24 pixel-identical after captions were excluded; Figures 30 and 31 have captions but no charts. The arXiv record, checked 2026-08-23, has no later revision and carries an administrator note of substantial text overlap with arXiv:1309.2388. Audited the first-party repository https://github.com/Tikquuss/sag_torch at current HEAD a4f5b1baa48ff449b15c604956e54da306d96ef5 (40 commits; last commit 2023-08-30T22:19:53-04:00). All ordinary Python files pass compileall, but no full training reproduction was claimed because the environment declaration is incomplete and no raw results or checkpoints are committed. Static analysis and minimal scalar probes verified the full-batch degeneration and the multi-batch normalization defect; code also confirms the initialization, double-decay, preprocessing, seed-flag, and CIFAR-100 defects described above. A plaintext W&B credential was found in tracked notebooks; its value is intentionally not reproduced and should be revoked and purged from history. Current primary competitors were checked through 2026-08-23, with special attention to direct momentum methods, adaptive variance reduction, negative deep-learning evidence, the nearly simultaneous AdaLVR submission, and the later large-model MARS framework.
